Question: Let \(S\) be the set of all points with coordinates \((x, y, z),\) where \(x,\) \(y,\) and \(z\) are each chosen from the set \(\{0, 1, 2\}.\) How many equilateral triangles have all their vertices in \(S?\)
Solution:
Squared distances are convenient because every coordinate difference is an integer. Let \(m>0\) be the common squared side length of an equilateral triangle with vertices in \(S\). Each coordinate difference has absolute value \(0,1\), or \(2\), so each squared contribution is \(0,1\), or \(4\).

First, \(m\) must be even. An integer and its square have the same parity, so the parity of a squared distance equals the parity of the difference between the two points' coordinate sums. Among three vertices, two coordinate sums have the same parity. Their squared distance is even, and all three squared distances equal \(m\).

The positive even sums of three members of \(\{0,1,4\}\) give
\[
m\in\{2,4,6,8,12\}.
\]
We can eliminate two of these possibilities.

If \(m=4\), a side has absolute coordinate differences \((2,0,0)\), in some order. Along its changing coordinate the endpoints are \(0\) and \(2\). If the third vertex has coordinate \(q\) there, equal distances to the endpoints require \(q^2=(q-2)^2\), so \(q=1\). Its other two squared coordinate differences would then have to sum to \(4-1=3\). That is impossible using two members of \(\{0,1,4\}\).

If \(m=12\), every coordinate difference along a side has absolute value \(2\), so its endpoints are opposite corners of the entire cube. From either corner there is only one point of \(S\) at squared distance 12, namely the other corner. A third vertex is therefore impossible.

Now count the remaining three cases.

For \(m=2\) or \(m=8\), write \(m=2t^2\), with \(t=1\) or \(t=2\). Every side has absolute coordinate differences \((t,t,0)\), in some order. Thus, in each coordinate, the vertices use at most two values separated by \(t\). No coordinate can be constant: otherwise all three vertices would have to be pairwise different in each of the other two coordinates, although only two values are available. Consequently the triangle's smallest box with edges parallel to the coordinate axes is a unique cube of side \(t\), and its vertices are corners of that cube.

To count triangles in one such cube, encode each lower coordinate value by \(0\) and each upper value by \(1\). Divide the eight corners into the four with even coordinate sum and the four with odd coordinate sum. Two distinct corners are in the same group exactly when they differ in two coordinates, giving squared distance \(2t^2\). Therefore every valid triangle uses three corners from one group, and any three corners from one group work. Each group gives four triangles, according to which corner is omitted, so each cube gives eight.

There are \(2\cdot2\cdot2=8\) cubes of side 1, giving \(8\cdot8=64\) triangles with \(m=2\). There is one cube of side 2, giving eight triangles with \(m=8\). The unique smallest cube ensures that these counts have no repetitions.

Finally, suppose \(m=6\). Every side has absolute coordinate differences \((2,1,1)\), in some order. All three coordinates change along every side, so each coordinate takes the three distinct values \(0,1,2\) across the vertices. In each coordinate, exactly one edge joins \(0\) to \(2\). Since each edge has a difference of 2 in exactly one coordinate, these three distinguished edges are different.

It follows that the vertex having \(x=1\), the vertex having \(y=1\), and the vertex having \(z=1\) are all different. Label them \(A,B,C\), respectively. In the \(x\)-coordinate, assign \(0\) and \(2\) to \(B,C\) in two ways. Independently, assign \(0,2\) to \(A,C\) in the \(y\)-coordinate and to \(A,B\) in the \(z\)-coordinate. This gives \(2^3=8\) choices. Every choice makes each side differ by 2 in one coordinate and by 1 in the other two, so all eight choices work. The labels are determined uniquely by the triangle, so each triangle is counted once.

The cases exhaust all possible squared side lengths. Hence the total is
\[
64+8+8=\boxed{80},
\]
choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).
